title: Celsus tells the story of Aristeas
source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ καὶ ἃ μετὰ ταῦτα λέγει ὁ Κέλσος, παρατιθέμενος ἀπὸ ἱστοριῶν παράδοξα καὶ καθ᾿ αὑτὰ μὲν ἀπίστοις ἐοικότα ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ δὲ οὐκ ἀπιστούμενα ὅσον γε ἐπὶ τῇ λέξει αὐτοῦ. καὶ πρῶτόν γε τὰ περὶ τὸν Προκοννήσιον Ἀριστέαν, περὶ οὗ ταῦτά φησιν· εἶτ᾿ Ἀριστέαν μὲν τὸν Προκοννήσιον ἀφανισθέντα τε οὕτως δαι μονίως ἐξ ἀνθρώπων καὶ αὖθις ἐναργῶς φανέντα καὶ πολλοῖς ὕστερον χρόνοις πολλαχοῦ τῆς οἰκουμένης ἐπιδημήσαντα καὶ θαυμαστὰ ἀγγείλαντα, καὶ τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος ἐπισκήψαντος Μεταποντίνοις ἐν θεῶν μοίρᾳ νέμειν τὸν Ἀριστέαν, τοῦτον οὐδεὶς ἔτι νομίζει θεόν. ἔοικε δ᾿ εἰληφέναι τὴν ἱστορίαν ἀπὸ Πινδάρου καὶ Ἡροδότου. ἀρκεῖ δὲ νῦν τὴν Ἡροδότου παραθέσθαι λέξιν ἀπὸ τῆς τετάρτης τῶν ἱστοριῶν οὕτως περὶ αὐτοῦ ἔχουσαν. „καὶ ὅθεν μὲν ἦν Ἀριστέης ὁ ταῦτα εἴπας, εἴρηκα· ὃν δὲ περὶ αὐτοῦ λόγον ἤκουον ἐν Προκοννήσῳ καὶ Κυζίκῳ, λέξω. Ἀριστέην γὰρ λέγουσιν ἐόντα τῶν ἀστῶν οὐδενὸς γένει ὑποδεέστερον, εἰσελθόντα ἐς κναφήιον ἐν Προκοννήσῳ ἀποθανεῖν· καὶ τὸν κναφέα κατακληΐσαντα τὸ ἐργαστήριον οἴχεσθαι ἀγγελέοντα τοῖς προσήκουσι τῷ νέκυϊ. ἐσκεδασμένου δὲ ἤδη τοῦ λόγου ἀνὰ τὴν πόλιν. ὡς τεθνεὼς εἴη (ὁ) Ἀριστέης, ἐς ἀμφισβασίας τοῖς λέγουσιν ἀπικέσθαι ἄνδρα Κυζικηνὸν ἥκοντα ἐξ Ἀρτάκης πόλιος, φάντα συντυχεῖν τε οἱ ἰόντι ἐπὶ Κυζίκου καὶ ἐς λόγους ἀπικέσθαι. καὶ τοῦτον μὲν ἐντεταμένως ἀμφισβατέειν, τοὺς δὲ προσήκοντας τῷ νέκυϊ ἐπὶ τὸ κναφήιον παρεῖναι ἔχοντας τὰ πρόσφορα ὡς ἀναιρησομένους· ἀνοιχθέντος δὲ τοῦ οἰκήματος οὔτε ζῶντα οὔτε τεθνεῶτα φαίνεσθαι Ἀριστέην. μετὰ δὲ ἑβδόμῳ ἔτεϊ φανέντα αὐτὸν ἐς Προκόννησον ποιῆσαι τὰ ἔπεα ταῦτα, ἃ δὴ νῦν ὑπὸ Ἑλλήνων Ἀριμάσπεια καλέεται, ποιήσαντα δὲ ἀφανισθῆναι τὸ δεύτερον. ταῦτα μὲν οὖν αἱ πόλιες αὗται λέγουσι· τάδε δὲ οἶδα Μεταποντίνοις τοῖς ἐν Ἰταλίῃ συγκυρήσαντα μετὰ τὴν ἀφάνισιν τὴν δευτέρην Ἀριστέω ἔτεσι τεσσαράκοντα καὶ διακοσίοις, ὡς ἐγὼ συμβαλλόμενος ἐν Προκοννήσῳ καὶ Μεταποντίῳ εὕρισκον. Μεταποντῖνοι δέ φασιν αὐτὸν Ἀριστέην φανέντα σφιν ἐς τὴν χώρην κελεῦσαι βωμὸν Ἀπόλλωνος (ἱδρύσασθαι) καὶ Ἀριστέω τοῦ Προκοννησίου ἐπωνυμίην ἔχοντα ἀνδριάντα παραστῆσαι. φάναι γάρ σφιν τὸν Ἀπόλλωνα Ἰταλιωτέων μούνοισι δὴ ἀπικέσθαι ἐς τὴν χώρην, καὶ αὐτός οἱ ἕπεσθαι ὁ νῦν ἐὼν Ἀριστέης· τότε δὲ, ὅτε εἵπετο τῷ θεῷ, εἶναι κόραξ. καὶ τὸν μὲν εἰπόντα ταῦτα ἀφανισθῆναι, σφέας δὲ Μεταποντῖνοι λέγουσιν ἐς Δελφοὺς πέμψαντας τὸν θεὸν ἐπερωτᾶν, ὅ τι τὸ φάσμα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου εἴη. τὴν δὲ Πυθίην σφέας κελεῦσαι πείθεσθαι τῷ φάσματι, πειθομένοισί τε ἄμεινον συνοίσεσθαι. καὶ σφέας δεξαμένους ταῦτα ποιῆσαι ἐπιτελέα. καὶ νῦν ἕστηκεν ἀνδριὰς ἐπωνυμίην ἔχων Ἀριστέω παρ᾿ αὐτῷ τῷ ἀγάλματι τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος, πέριξ δὲ αὐτὸν δάφναι εἰσί· τὸ δὲ ἄγαλμα ἐν τῇ ἀγορῇ ἵδρυται. Ἀριστέω μέν νυν πέρι τοσαῦτα εἰρήσθω.“
pass_a_gloss: Let us see (ὁράω) also what Celsus says after these things, setting beside (παρατίθημι) from histories (ἱστορίαι) marvels (παράδοξα), in themselves resembling unbelievable things (ἄπιστα), but not disbelieved (ἀπιστέω) by him, at least as far as his wording (λέξις). And first the things about Aristeas of Proconnesus, about whom he says this: 'Then Aristeas the Proconnesian, having vanished (ἀφανίζω) so supernaturally (δαιμονίως) from among men and again having appeared (φαίνω) plainly (ἐναργῶς), and many times later having visited (ἐπιδημέω) many places of the inhabited world (οἰκουμένη) and having reported (ἀγγέλλω) wonderful things, and Apollo having enjoined (ἐπισκήπτω) the Metapontines to assign (νέμω) Aristeas in the portion of the gods (ἐν θεῶν μοίρᾳ) — this one no one still/any longer (ἔτι) considers (νομίζω) a god.' He seems to have taken the story from Pindar and Herodotus. It suffices now to set beside the wording of Herodotus from the fourth of the Histories, holding thus about him: 'And whence Aristeas was, who said these things, I have said; the account (λόγος) I heard about him in Proconnesus and Cyzicus I will tell. They say Aristeas, being by birth (γένος) inferior to none of the townsmen (ἀστοί), having gone into a fuller's shop (κναφήιον) in Proconnesus, died; and the fuller (κναφεύς), having locked (κατακληΐω) the workshop, went off to announce it to those related (προσήκοντες) to the dead man (νέκυς). The report being already scattered through the city that Aristeas had died, there came into dispute (ἀμφισβασίη) with those saying it a Cyzicene man coming from the city of Artace, saying that he met (συντυγχάνω) him going toward Cyzicus and came into talk with him. And this man disputed (ἀμφισβατέω) intensely (ἐντεταμένως), and the relatives of the dead man were at the fuller's shop having the fitting things (τὰ πρόσφορα) as to take up (ἀναιρέω) the body; but the room (οἴκημα) being opened, Aristeas appeared neither living nor dead. And in the seventh year, having appeared in Proconnesus, he made these verses (ἔπεα) which now by the Greeks are called Arimaspea, and having made them vanished the second time. These things these cities say; but these I know befell (συγκυρέω) the Metapontines in Italy after the second disappearance (ἀφάνισις) of Aristeas by two hundred and forty years, as I, putting together (συμβάλλομαι) in Proconnesus and Metapontum, found. The Metapontines say Aristeas himself, having appeared to them in their land (χώρη), ordered (κελεύω) to set up an altar (βωμός) of Apollo and to set beside it a statue (ἀνδριάς) having the name (ἐπωνυμίη) of Aristeas the Proconnesian. For he said to them that Apollo had come to their land alone of the Italiotes, and he himself followed him, he who now is Aristeas; but then, when he followed the god, he was a raven (κόραξ). And he having said these things vanished, and the Metapontines say they, having sent to Delphi, asked the god what the apparition (φάσμα) of the man might be. And the Pythia ordered them to obey (πείθομαι) the apparition, and that for them obeying it would turn out better (ἄμεινον συνοίσεσθαι). And they, having received these things, made them accomplished (ἐπιτελέα). And now there stands a statue having the name of Aristeas beside the very image (ἄγαλμα) of Apollo, and around it are laurels (δάφναι); and the image is set up in the marketplace (ἀγορή). About Aristeas let so much be said.'
pass_b_english: Let us see also what Celsus says after this, as he sets out marvels from the histories which in themselves look incredible, yet which he does not disbelieve, at least so far as his words go. First comes the story of Aristeas of Proconnesus, about whom he says this: "Then Aristeas of Proconnesus: he vanished from among men in so supernatural a way, appeared again plainly, long afterwards visited many parts of the world and reported marvels, and Apollo enjoined the Metapontines to count Aristeas among the gods; yet no one any longer regards this man as a god."

He seems to have taken the story from Pindar and Herodotus. For now it is enough to set out the words of Herodotus from the fourth book of his Histories, which run thus about him (Herodotus, Histories 4.14–15): "Where Aristeas, who said these things, came from, I have told; and the account I heard of him in Proconnesus and Cyzicus I shall tell. They say that Aristeas, who was inferior in birth to none of the citizens, went into a fuller's shop in Proconnesus and died there, and that the fuller locked up his workshop and went off to tell the dead man's relatives. When the report that Aristeas was dead had already spread through the city, a man of Cyzicus who had come from the town of Artace disputed it with those who were saying it, declaring that he had met Aristeas as he was going toward Cyzicus and had spoken with him. While he was disputing it hotly, the dead man's relatives came to the fuller's shop with what was needed to take up the body; but when the room was opened, Aristeas was to be seen neither alive nor dead. In the seventh year afterwards he appeared in Proconnesus and composed the verses which the Greeks now call the Arimaspea, and having composed them he vanished a second time.

"This is what these cities say. But this I know happened to the Metapontines in Italy two hundred and forty years after the second disappearance of Aristeas, as I found by reckoning in Proconnesus and in Metapontum. The Metapontines say that Aristeas himself appeared to them in their country and bade them set up an altar to Apollo, and beside it a statue bearing the name of Aristeas of Proconnesus. For he told them that theirs was the only country of all the Italian Greeks to which Apollo had come, and that he himself, who was now Aristeas, was following him; but at that time, when he followed the god, he was a raven. Having said this he vanished; and the Metapontines say that they sent to Delphi and asked the god what the apparition of the man might be. The Pythia bade them obey the apparition, saying that if they obeyed, it would go better for them. They accepted this and carried it out. And to this day there stands a statue bearing the name of Aristeas beside the very image of Apollo, with laurels around it; the image is set up in the marketplace. So much, then, for Aristeas."

choices.choice: Celsus's fragment opens with εἶτ' and an accusative left hanging (Ἀριστέαν ... τοῦτον οὐδεὶς ἔτι νομίζει θεόν), probably one item in a list of wonder-workers set against Jesus; rendered 'Then Aristeas of Proconnesus: ...; yet no one ...'. 'yet' renders the concessive force of the genitive absolute (Apollo's command). ἔτι rendered 'any longer'; 'still no one' is also possible. δαιμονίως rendered 'supernatural' (it is Celsus's word, not a judgement that demons were at work). The Herodotus quotation is Histories 4.14-15, quoted in Ionic; Koetschau's supplements (ὁ) and (ἱδρύσασθαι) are followed. The text cited by Origen reads 'two hundred and forty years'; the Pindar source is not extant and is not cited. 'Italiotes' rendered 'Italian Greeks'. No Scripture in this chapter. Reviewer: Celsus's εἶτ' with the hanging accusative may also be read as an indignant question ('And then is no one any longer to regard Aristeas ... as a god?'); the statement form keeps the same sense and is left.
Celsus: 'many years later' -> 'long afterwards' (πολλοῖς ὕστερον χρόνοις; the Greek names no years)

'For he said that of all the Italian Greeks Apollo had come to their country alone' -> 'For he told them that theirs was the only country of all the Italian Greeks to which Apollo had come' (μούνοισι agrees with the Metapontines, not Apollo; old wording could still be read as 'Apollo alone'; σφιν = 'told them')

checked unchanged: Celsus's words inside double quotation marks and 'he says' framing kept; Herodotus quotation runs 4.14.1 'καὶ ὅθεν μὲν ἦν Ἀριστέης' to 4.15.4 'τοσαῦτα εἰρήσθω', inline citation correct; Koetschau supplements (ὁ), (ἱδρύσασθαι) followed; οἱ ἰόντι correctly refers to Aristeas; 240 years kept
